readings.title: Donald and Dorothy: In Which None of the Characters Appear (Chapter I)
readings.challenge: Work out what is happening from sounds alone, as the dog outside the door must.
readings.focus: A mystery opening: a man writes something behind a closed door, rings, and leaves, and the only witness is a dog.
readings.context: Donald and Dorothy (1883) is by Mary Mapes Dodge, author of Hans Brinker and editor of St. Nicholas, a famous magazine for children. This very short first chapter is a puzzle that the rest of the book will explain, so read it twice. A quill pen is made from a feather; a bell-pull rang a bell in the servants’ part of the house; “at half-mast” means drooping, like a flag lowered halfway.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, “In Which None of the Characters Appear,” the whole chapter; opens “The door of the study was closed, and only Nero was to be seen. He, poor dog, stood in…”; closes “…settled down on the rug before the study fire. For there was not a soul in the room.”.

questions.prompt: What does Nero hear through the door? List the sounds in order. What might the man be doing?
facilitatorNotes: Steps, a chair drawn to the table, rustling paper, a deep moan, a quill scratching fast, then silence. He seems to be writing something important and painful, perhaps a letter or a will; the moan suggests sorrow.
evidence: a deep-voiced moan; the rapid scratching of a quill pen

questions.prompt: How does the narrator show what Nero feels without the dog saying a word?
facilitatorNotes: His ears prick up, he droops “at half-mast,” his tail wags like a machine-crank meant to pull Liddy upstairs, he takes an “agonized glance,” and at last gives a deep sigh. Each movement shows a feeling.
evidence: poor Nero again stood at half-mast
as though it were the crank of some unseen machine

questions.prompt: The title says none of the characters appear, and the chapter ends, “For there was not a soul in the room.” Why might an author begin a book this way?
facilitatorNotes: To build a mystery: we do not know who the man is or what he wrote, and must wait to find out. The “dignified legs” are the only clue to who he is. Some readers will find this frustrating; others will want to read on.
evidence: For there was not a soul in the room.
a pair of dignified legs moving toward the great hall door

readings.title: Donald and Dorothy: muffins and a puzzling uncle (Chapters V and VI, first part)
readings.challenge: Notice small signs that an adult is troubled, and keep track of them.
readings.focus: Uncle George begins an important talk, but keeps reacting strangely to Dorothy.
readings.context: Donald and Dorothy (1883) is by Mary Mapes Dodge, author of Hans Brinker and editor of St. Nicholas, a famous magazine for children. Fourteen-year-old twins Donald and Dorothy Reed (“the D’s”) live at Lakewood with their Uncle George. Their father died in England, and their mother was lost at sea when they were six weeks old; the babies were saved from the shipwreck by Jack, who now works for the family. Liddy (Lydia) is the housekeeper and Nero the old dog. That afternoon, on a drive, Dorothy saw a tall, thin stranger who has been hanging about the place. Trig means neat; perturbed means upset; a conference is a serious meeting; to domineer is to boss.

excerpt.locator: Chapter V, “Supper-Time,” whole, and Chapter VI, “A Family Conference,” through the twins’ exact age; opens “"OH, if gentlemen only knew the nature of muffins!"”; closes “"Yes, sir, right to a minute," replied Donald, laughing.”.

questions.prompt: Why is Liddy anxious at the start, and what does the joke about muffins show?
facilitatorNotes: Uncle George is late, and muffins must be eaten hot. The narrator makes fun of her worry, then lets her be satisfied: he does “appreciate the nature of muffins.” It is a light start before a serious talk.
evidence: if gentlemen only knew the nature of muffins
did appreciate the nature of muffins

questions.prompt: When Dorothy asks, “Did he know Aunt Kate?” how does everyone react, and what does that suggest?
facilitatorNotes: Donald looks frightened, Uncle George coughs, and Dorothy feels she can never mention her aunt “without raising a storm.” The subject is clearly painful for her uncle.
evidence: Donald looked frightened; Uncle George coughed
never to be able to speak of your own aunty without raising a storm

questions.prompt: Why does Uncle George suddenly pull his arm away and tell Dorothy to stop her nonsense? What does Donald think?
facilitatorNotes: Something in Dorothy’s manner upsets him, and Donald thinks “Uncle’s afraid again,” not angry. Readers may guess that she reminds him of someone, or that he is worried about something he has not said.
evidence: Now Uncle's afraid again
felt her uncle's arm immediately withdrawn

questions.prompt: Why is Dorothy glad that she and Donald are exactly the same age?
facilitatorNotes: Because neither twin can boss the other; they start “fair and square.” It shows how much she values being Donald’s equal.
evidence: twins can't boss--I mean domineer--each other

readings.title: Donald and Dorothy: boarding school, a stranger and a tutor (Chapter VI, second part)
readings.challenge: Separate what Uncle George says from what he seems to be hiding.
readings.focus: Uncle George keeps Donald at home, warns the twins about a stranger, and tells them their tutor must leave.
readings.context: Recap: after supper Uncle George called the twins into the library for a serious talk, but kept stopping, and seemed troubled whenever Dorothy spoke of Aunt Kate. Apprehended here means feared; a ne’er-do-weel is a good-for-nothing; rudiments are first lessons; a tutor teaches children at home.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VI, “A Family Conference,” from the talk of boarding-school to Uncle George’s plan to release Dr. Lane; opens “"Well, there is no hurry, I am glad to say. I have been thinking of late, Donald, that a…”; closes “…doctor the very next morning, if they would let him know when the lesson-hours were over.”.

questions.prompt: What does Donald imagine about boarding school, and what spoils the picture?
facilitatorNotes: A crack baseball club, a debating society, boxes of cake from home, even a fight or two; but he cannot imagine living without Dorry.
evidence: to get boxes of fruit and cake from home
but then how strange it would be to live without Dorry!

questions.prompt: Dorothy expects a warning about matches and bonfires. What is the warning really about, and what are the rules?
facilitatorNotes: The “long and lank” stranger. They must avoid him, never let him think they fear him, stay inside the gates and keep together.
evidence: Do not fear this man. Above all, do not let him imagine that you fear him.
Keep within the gates for the present.

questions.prompt: What does Uncle George tell the twins about the stranger, and what does he refuse to explain?
facilitatorNotes: He knew the man as a boy, and thinks he has been “going down for years.” He will not say why they must avoid him: “You need not see, nor try to see.” Readers may predict a link with the family’s past.
evidence: He is a ne'er-do-weel, whom I knew as a boy
You need not see, nor try to see.

questions.prompt: Dorothy cries “No more old algebra!” and then begs that Dr. Lane go at once. Is she selfish or kind? How does Donald know?
facilitatorNotes: Her first thought was a holiday, but she truly wants him to get well in the south, and Donald knows her well enough to see that she means it. A reader could call her both, one after the other.
evidence: Her vivid imagination had instantly pictured relief and a grand holiday.
She was thoroughly sincere and full of sympathy

readings.title: Donald and Dorothy: Uncle George weeps (Chapter VI, third part)
readings.challenge: Listen to a character who says more than she meant to, and watch its effect.
readings.focus: Dorothy pours out her longing for a mother, and the twins learn what the shipwreck took from their uncle too.
readings.context: Recap: Uncle George has told the twins that Donald will not go to boarding school yet, warned them to avoid a stranger, and said their tutor must leave. Each time Dorothy mentioned Aunt Kate, he grew upset. A likeness is a portrait; impetuous means acting on sudden feeling; to reproach is to blame.
readings.contentNote: The family history is one of deaths: the twins’ father died in England, and their mother, aunt, uncle and baby cousin were lost at sea.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VI, “A Family Conference,” from Donald’s question about boarding-school to Uncle George’s “Bless you, my little comforter”; opens “"Uncle!"”; closes “…my little comforter!--No. God be praised, we still have a great deal to be thankful for."”.

questions.prompt: Why does Dorothy say she has to ask about Aunt Kate? What is she really asking for?
facilitatorNotes: She is a girl with no mother and wants to know the women of her family; her mother’s portrait looks stiff to her, while Aunt Kate’s picture seems sweet and alive. She is asking for a mother’s story.
evidence: it's so hard, so awfully hard, to be a girl without any mother!
Aunt Kate's picture in the parlor is so different

questions.prompt: Dorothy starts to promise she will not be “so wicked again,” but stops. Why?
facilitatorNotes: She knows she has not been wicked, only quick to speak, so she will not say what is untrue even to apologise. She chooses a better word, “impetuous.”
evidence: She knew that she had not been wicked, and yet she could not at first hit upon the right term.

questions.prompt: What do the twins and their uncle say about the family’s past? Who was on the ship that went down?
facilitatorNotes: Their father died in England before he could sail. Their mother, Aunt Kate, Uncle Robertson and baby cousin Delia were all aboard, and the ship sank. Uncle George had hardly known the twins’ mother.
evidence: because he never lived to set sail from England
if the ship had landed safe

questions.prompt: How does Dorothy comfort her uncle, and does it work?
facilitatorNotes: She turns from what was lost to what they still have: the three of them together. He calls her his “little comforter” and gives thanks, so it does help.
evidence: It can't be so very miserable and dreadful with you and Donald and me left!
Bless you, my little comforter!

readings.title: Donald and Dorothy: Jack the rescuer, and a man at the door (Chapter VI, end)
readings.challenge: Notice how characters tell a story they cannot really remember.
readings.focus: The twins retell their rescue at sea, then see the stranger outside at bedtime.
readings.context: Recap: in a tearful talk, Uncle George told the twins how much he had lost when their family’s ship went down, and Dorothy comforted him. A trump is a fine, dependable person; to capsize is to turn over; balusters are the posts of a stair rail; an edict is an order; remonstrances are protests.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VI, “A Family Conference,” from Donald’s mention of Liddy, Jack and Nero to the end of the chapter; opens “"Yes, and there are Liddy and Jack, and dear old Nero," said Donald, partly because he…”; closes “…minutes,--a great while for her,--thinking over the events of the day and evening.”.

questions.prompt: How can the twins describe the shipwreck when they were only six weeks old?
facilitatorNotes: They have talked about it so often that they feel they remember it; the narrator says so in brackets. Their argument about whether babies play pat-a-cake shows they are imagining.
evidence: The children had talked about the shipwreck so often that they felt as if they remembered the awful scene.
babies only six weeks old playing pat-a-cake! I guess not.

questions.prompt: What did Jack do to save them? Which act seems bravest to you?
facilitatorNotes: He caught the babies tossed from the ship, threw them into a boat, plunged back into the sea to save others, returned alone and half dead, and then cared for them until another ship picked them up. Readers may choose different acts.
evidence: plunging into the sea to save all he could, but able to get back alone, after all
wrapped us in blankets, and fed us

questions.prompt: The narrator says Dorothy’s joke about the rescue was in bad taste. Why does she make it anyway?
facilitatorNotes: She has had enough sad seriousness for one evening and jokes “in pure defiance” of it. Readers may sympathise with her need to lighten the mood, or agree with the narrator.
evidence: she had spoken in pure defiance of solemnity
There had been quite enough of that for one evening.

questions.prompt: Why did Donald open his window and cough? What does Dorothy’s goodnight show?
facilitatorNotes: He wanted his uncle to know he was near if there was trouble with the stranger. Dorothy teases “how good we are,” but kisses him soberly and lies awake: she is worried too.
evidence: You coughed, just to let Uncle know that you were around, if there should be any trouble.
but she kissed Donald soberly for good-night
